steps.title: Import required modules
steps.instruction: Import the http and url modules from Node.js to create an HTTP server and parse request URLs.
steps.hint: Use the require() function to import Node.js built-in modules. Both modules are built into Node.js, so you don't need to install anything.
steps.seedCode: // Import the http and url modules here
steps.expectedOutcome: The http and url modules are imported and ready to use for building the long polling endpoint.
successCriteria: Both http and url modules are imported using require() statements.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported the required modules. The http module will help create the server, and url will help parse incoming request URLs.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but you need to import both modules. Make sure you're using require() for both http and url.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to import two built-in Node.js modules: http for creating the server and url for parsing URLs. Use require() statements for both.

steps.title: Create HTTP server
steps.instruction: Create an HTTP server using the imported http module's createServer method and store it in a variable named 'server'.
steps.hint: Call http.createServer() and assign the result to a const variable named 'server'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Creating a basic HTTP server
const server = http.createServer();
steps.seedCode:
// Import the http and url modules here

// Create your HTTP server here
steps.expectedOutcome: An HTTP server instance is created and stored in the 'server' variable.
successCriteria: The server variable is declared using const and assigned the result of http.createServer().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created an HTTP server instance.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using http.createServer() and storing it in a variable named 'server'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Use http.createServer() to create the server and store it in a variable named 'server'.

steps.title: Initialize polling data store
steps.instruction: Create an empty array to store pending client requests that are waiting for updates. Place this array at the top of your file, after the imports but before the server creation.
steps.hint: You can create an empty array using const pendingRequests = [];
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating an empty array for storing data
const todoList = [];
steps.expectedOutcome: An empty array variable is created to track pending long polling requests.
successCriteria: An empty array named pendingRequests (or similar) is declared and initialized.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the data store for tracking pending requests.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created an array, but make sure it's empty and named appropriately for tracking pending requests.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try creating an empty array variable to store pending client requests.

steps.title: Parse request URL
steps.instruction: Inside the server's request handler, use the url module to parse the request URL and extract the pathname. Store the parsed URL object in a variable called 'parsedUrl'.
steps.hint: Use the url.parse() method with the request's URL string. Then access the parsedUrl.pathname property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will now parse incoming request URLs to identify different endpoints.
successCriteria: The request handler includes a 'parsedUrl' variable that stores the result of url.parse(req.url).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully parsed the request URL. This will let you identify different endpoints like /poll and /data.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using url.parse() with req.url and storing the result in a variable named 'parsedUrl'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The URL parsing isn't quite right. Use the url module's parse() method on the request URL.

steps.title: Handle long polling endpoint
steps.instruction: Inside the request handler, check if the parsed URL pathname is '/poll'. If it is, push the response object into the pendingRequests array.
steps.hint: You can access the pathname from parsedUrl.pathname. Use an if statement to compare it with '/poll'. The pendingRequests array was created in step 3.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will now recognize requests to '/poll' and store their response objects for later use.
successCriteria: The code includes an if statement that checks parsedUrl.pathname === '/poll' and pushes the res object into pendingRequests.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully set up the route detection for long polling requests. The server will now capture client connections to '/poll'.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking the pathname property and pushing the response object (res) into the array.
steps.feedbackWrong: The long polling endpoint isn't properly configured. Check that you're comparing parsedUrl.pathname with '/poll' and storing the response object.

steps.title: Set response headers
steps.instruction: Inside the long polling request handler, set the response headers to 'Content-Type: application/json' and add CORS headers to allow cross-origin requests.
steps.hint: Use res.setHeader() to set headers. You'll need to set 'Content-Type' and 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' headers.
steps.expectedOutcome: The long polling endpoint will properly configure headers for JSON responses and CORS support.
successCriteria: Response headers are set with 'Content-Type: application/json' and 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' inside the polling handler.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've properly configured the response headers for the long polling endpoint.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've set some headers, but make sure to include both 'Content-Type' and CORS headers.
steps.feedbackWrong: The headers aren't set correctly. Check that you're using res.setHeader() inside the polling handler.

steps.title: Handle data update endpoint
steps.instruction: Add an else-if condition to check if the request path is '/update' and send data to all pending polling requests.
steps.hint: Use parsedUrl.pathname to check for '/update'. Inside the condition, iterate through pendingRequests and send a response to each.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will now have an endpoint that can trigger updates for all waiting clients.
successCriteria: An else-if condition checks for '/update' and sends a response to each pending request.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the update endpoint that will send data to all waiting clients.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking for '/update' and iterating through pendingRequests.
steps.feedbackWrong: The update endpoint isn't implemented correctly. Check the pathname and ensure you're responding to all pending requests.

steps.title: Send responses to waiting clients
steps.instruction: Inside the '/update' endpoint handler, add a loop that iterates through the pendingRequests array and sends a JSON response to each waiting client with the updated data, then clears the array.
steps.hint: Use a for loop or forEach to go through each response object in pendingRequests. For each response, use res.writeHead() with status 200 and Content-Type: application/json, then res.end() with JSON.stringify() containing the new data.
steps.expectedOutcome: When data is updated via the /update endpoint, all waiting long polling clients receive a JSON response with the new data, and the pendingRequests array is emptied.
successCriteria: The code includes a loop that iterates over pendingRequests, sends a JSON response with status 200 and Content-Type header to each, and clears the array after sending.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've implemented the response sending mechanism. Now when data updates, all waiting clients will receive the new data immediately.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the loop, but make sure to send proper JSON responses with headers and clear the pending array after.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the structure: you need to loop through pendingRequests, send a JSON response to each, then clear the array.

steps.title: Handle other routes
steps.instruction: Add an else block after your existing if/else-if conditions to send a 404 response for any request that doesn't match '/poll' or '/update' endpoints.
steps.hint: After your else-if block for '/update', add else { ... } with res.writeHead(404) and res.end().
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will respond with a 404 status for any request to paths other than '/poll' or '/update'.
successCriteria: An else block is added after the existing conditions, containing res.writeHead(404) and res.end().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a default 404 response for unmatched routes, making your server more robust.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added an else block, but make sure it includes both res.writeHead(404) and res.end().
steps.feedbackWrong: The else block for handling other routes is missing or incomplete.

steps.title: Test the long polling server
steps.instruction: Start the server by running the code, then test both the polling endpoint and the update endpoint to see the long polling in action.
steps.hint: You can test the endpoints by opening two browser tabs: one to http://localhost:3000/poll (which will wait) and another to http://localhost:3000/update (which will trigger the response).
steps.expectedOutcome: The server starts successfully and you can test the long polling behavior by making requests to /poll and /update endpoints.
successCriteria: Server starts without errors and both endpoints respond appropriately when tested.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully started the server and tested the long polling endpoints. The server is now running and ready to handle client requests.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the server, but make sure to test both endpoints to verify the long polling behavior works correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The server may not have started correctly or the endpoints aren't responding as expected. Check the console for errors and verify your implementation.
